title: How to keep reading
hook: you've read Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, the prophets, two gospels and three letters

segments.voice: Yesterday, two short notes from the elder, and your line was face to face. Who did you see in person instead of on a screen? Day six hundred ninety-four.

Look at what you've read this year. Genesis, from the garden to Joseph's tears. Exodus, from the brick kilns to the mountain. The Psalms and the wisdom books. The prophets, with their burning coal and their valley of dry bones. Luke, start to finish. John, start to finish. Philippians, James, and the letters of the elder. That's a big piece of a big book. And it raises an honest question that comes up at exactly this point: when the lessons stop walking you through it, how do you keep reading?
screen: `A BIG PIECE OF A BIG BOOK.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, which means the books. Plural. It isn't one book; it's a library, written over many centuries in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek: poems, laws, letters, stories, songs and visions. Churches even shelve it a little differently. Protestant Bibles usually have sixty-six books, Catholic Bibles seventy-three, and Orthodox Bibles a few more. So the first tip is the one every library teaches: you don't have to read the shelves in order. Christians have found many ways in. Some follow a lectionary, a set of readings for each day or each Sunday, so a whole congregation hears the same passage the same week. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many other churches use one. Some follow a reading plan, a few chapters a day, through the whole Bible in a year. And some read very slowly. For centuries, monks have practiced lectio divina, holy reading: a short passage, read again and again, until one word catches and stays. The second tip: read with someone. The first churches heard these books read aloud, together; most people couldn't own a copy. A friend, a group, a church study, even one person who texts you a verse each morning keeps the book open. And the third: expect it to keep surprising you. A psalm read at twenty reads differently at fifty. Here is a verse from Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for your feet, not a floodlight for the whole road. Enough light for the next step, and then the next.
screen: `A LECTIONARY, A PLAN, A SLOW PAGE.`
then, large: `A LIGHT UNTO MY PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your next book. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the year. Which part pulled at you? If you loved the stories, you might try Acts, the story of the first churches, or Ruth, just four short chapters. If the Psalms spoke to you, you could keep one psalm a day. If you want more of Jesus, Mark is short and fast, and Matthew holds the Sermon on the Mount. Don't pick the hardest one. Pick the one you'll actually open. Then picture where and when: a chair, a time of day, a lamp. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart as you read. The bell holds the time.
How to keep reading. A library, not a single book: a lectionary, a plan or one slow page, ideally with someone beside you.
Your line: the book keeps opening. Today, read the first few verses of the book you chose, and stop where something catches. Day six hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians read the Bible through a church lectionary, a yearly reading plan, or slow prayerful reading such as lectio divina, often in a small group or alongside their congregation's Sunday readings.

fork.setup: you've finished a year of reading, and the lessons stop guiding you. what do you do?
options: start again at Genesis 1 and push through to the end.

fork.reveal: Christians read in many ways, and any of them can work. the tips here: pick the book you'll actually open, and don't read alone.

original.note: Greek: books, the plural of biblion. the word behind our word Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: one long book, to be read front to back.
what it means: a library of many books, and Christians read it by lectionary, by plan, or slowly, often together.
what a scholar hears: ta biblia, the books, plural; and different canons: 66 books in most Protestant Bibles, 73 in Catholic ones, more in Orthodox.
